title: AI Unlocked: NGOs & Nonprofits
blurb: For NGO leaders and program staff: grant-winning proposal engines, donor reporting on autopilot, M&E acceleration, low-bandwidth field workflows, and safeguarding-aware data ethics — built by a practitioner who has strengthened NGO systems on three continents.

modules.d: Where AI genuinely multiplies a nonprofit's capacity — and where it creates new risks.
modules.body:
The capacity gap AI can close

Most NGOs operate with a structural gap between what their mission requires and what their staffing allows. Programme officers write proposals at night, M&E staff hand-clean survey data, communications are an afterthought, and donor reports consume weeks that should go to beneficiaries. AI does not close that gap by replacing staff; it closes it by removing the low-value hours from skilled people's days so they can spend them on relationships, judgement and field presence — the things donors and communities actually value.

Mapping the NGO value chain

Think of the organisation as a chain: resource mobilisation (donor research, proposals, relationship management), programme design (needs assessment, theory of change, budgets), delivery (training, outreach, logistics), monitoring, evaluation and learning (data collection, analysis, reporting), communications (stories, social media, newsletters), and operations (finance, HR, procurement, compliance). AI assistance is strongest where work is text-heavy, repetitive and reviewable — drafting, summarising, translating, classifying qualitative data, formatting reports. It is weakest — and riskiest — where work requires local trust, verified facts about real people, or decisions affecting beneficiaries' safety or eligibility.

The 70/30 rule of thumb. Use AI to produce the first 70% of a draft — structure, language, consistency — then invest the human 30% where it matters: facts, figures, local context, donor-specific nuance and ethics. Organisations that reverse this ratio, letting AI produce the final 30%, are the ones that end up submitting proposals with invented statistics.

The adoption ladder

NGOs that adopt AI successfully tend to climb in stages. Stage 1 — Individual productivity: staff use a general AI assistant for drafting and summarising, with basic rules on what data may not be entered. Stage 2 — Shared workflows: the organisation builds reusable prompts, templates and a content library (organisational profile, past results, standard budget notes). Stage 3 — Integrated systems: AI is connected to the organisation's data — survey platforms, CRM, finance — with defined controls. Stage 4 — Strategic advantage: AI enables things previously impossible, such as analysing thousands of beneficiary feedback messages in local languages within days. Skipping stages, especially jumping to integrated systems without data governance, is the most common failure.

New risks the leveraged NGO must manage

  • Fabrication: AI generates plausible statistics, citations and quotes. In a proposal or donor report this is a credibility and potentially a fraud risk.
  • Beneficiary data exposure: entering names, health status, location or protection cases into consumer AI tools can breach consent, national law and donor requirements.
  • Homogenised voice: donors read hundreds of proposals; AI-generic language makes yours indistinguishable. Authentic field evidence and community voice are your differentiators.
  • Dependency and deskilling: junior staff who never learn to write a theory of change cannot judge whether AI wrote a good one.
  • Donor policies: some funders now ask applicants to disclose AI use or restrict it; always check the call's rules.

Theory of change for your own AI adoption

Apply the discipline you use for programmes to your adoption. If staff are trained and given safe tools and shared templates, then time spent on drafting and reporting falls, so that more time goes to field work and donor relationships, leading to stronger programmes and more sustainable funding. Define indicators — hours saved per proposal, proposals submitted per quarter, win rate, report turnaround time — and measure before and after.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as an NGO capacity advisor. Ask me about my organisation's size, programmes, funding sources and current bottlenecks. Map our value chain and identify the five highest-value, lowest-risk AI use cases, with the hours each could save. Then place us on the four-stage adoption ladder and give me a 90-day plan to reach the next stage, including the data rules staff must follow.

📚 Glossary

  • Value chain: the sequence of activities from fundraising to delivery to reporting
  • Adoption ladder: individual use → shared workflows → integrated systems → strategic advantage
  • Fabrication: AI-generated content that sounds factual but is invented
  • Theory of change: the causal pathway from activities to long-term impact

📖 References

  • NTEN — Nonprofit technology and AI adoption resources.
  • Stanford Social Innovation Review — articles on AI in the social sector.
  • Weiss, C. — Theory-based evaluation and theory of change.
  • Team21 Academy, AI Unlocked Level 1 curriculum.

quiz.q: A health NGO in Bamenda with no AI rules plans to connect an AI tool to its beneficiary case database next month to 'save the most time'. Its director asks for advice on sequencing.
opts: Start with staff drafting under basic data rules, then build shared templates before any system integration
Proceed with the integration but strip names from the case records before the connection goes live first
Integrate now, since the case database is where the largest share of staff hours is being lost
Pause AI use until a full national data protection audit of the organisation has been completed
quiz.x: The adoption ladder runs individual use with data rules, then shared workflows, then integration; skipping to integration without governance is the most common failure. Removing names is a partial fix: combinations of other fields can still identify people.

quiz.q: A programme officer in Nairobi uses AI to draft a concept note. The draft says malnutrition 'fell 23% after similar interventions in 2022' with no source. The deadline is in two days.
opts: Soften it to 'around 20%' so the claim is conservative and less likely to be challenged
Ask the AI tool to supply the citation it used so the reference list is complete before submission
Search for a real source for the figure and remove or replace the claim if none is found
Keep the figure but add a footnote noting that it is an AI-generated estimate for reviewers
quiz.x: AI fabricates plausible statistics and citations; every figure must trace to a verifiable source. Asking the AI for its citation is the tempting runner-up, but it can invent a reference just as easily as the number.

quiz.q: A youth NGO in Douala spends 40 staff hours per proposal. Leadership wants AI to write complete proposals so staff 'just press submit'. Which division of labour reflects the module's guidance?
opts: Staff write everything by hand and AI is used to translate the final version into French for donors
AI handles the final polish and formatting while staff write the substance from scratch as before
AI writes the full proposal and one senior manager signs it off after a quick read the day before each time
AI produces structure and first-draft language; staff invest their effort in facts, context and ethics
quiz.x: The 70/30 rule: AI does the first 70% (structure, language, consistency) and humans invest the critical 30% in facts, figures, context and ethics. Using AI just for polish wastes most of the gain; reversing the ratio is how invented statistics get submitted.

quiz.q: A US foundation's new call for proposals includes a clause on applicants' use of generative AI. A Cameroonian NGO's grants team already drafts every section with AI. What should they do first?
opts: Rewrite the AI sections in a different style so the foundation's reviewers cannot detect them
Read the clause and follow its disclosure or restriction rules before drafting this application
Carry on as usual, since a well-reviewed AI draft is the organisation's own intellectual work here
Stop using AI for proposals across all donors until each funder has published a formal policy
quiz.x: Some funders require disclosure or restrict AI use, so each call's rules must be checked and followed. Halting AI for every donor overreacts; disguising the use breaches honesty with donors.

quiz.q: Two NGO staff compare AI use. Aminata drafts newsletters and translates public reports; Paul pastes protection case notes into a free chatbot to summarise them. Which pairing of risk levels is accurate?
opts: Paul's use is acceptable if he deletes the chat afterwards; Aminata's raises copyright concerns each time
Both are high risk because any AI use with organisational material needs board approval first
Aminata's use is low risk; Paul's exposes sensitive beneficiary data and may breach consent and law
Both are low risk as long as each staff member reviews the AI output carefully before using it
quiz.x: Text-heavy, reviewable public work is where AI is strongest; protection case data in consumer tools risks breaching consent, national law and donor requirements. Deleting the chat afterwards does not undo the exposure.

quiz.q: Reviewers at an EU delegation note that three NGO proposals for the same call read almost identically: polished, generic and full of buzzwords. What differentiator does the module say each NGO lost?
opts: Authentic field evidence and community voice that show the organisation's particular knowledge
A larger number of academic citations showing that the design follows international best practice
Longer sections that address every evaluation criterion in more detail than competing applicants
Professional formatting with infographics that make the proposal stand out on the reviewer's desk
quiz.x: Homogenised AI voice makes proposals indistinguishable; real field evidence and community voice are the differentiators. More length or citations does not restore distinctiveness and can add fabrication risk.

quiz.q: An NGO manager in Accra wants to show the board that AI adoption is working. Which indicator set best matches the theory of change for AI adoption taught in the module?
opts: Staff satisfaction with AI tools, number of training sessions held and number of tools tested
Number of staff with AI accounts, number of prompts sent per week and monthly subscription spend
Social media followers, newsletter open rate and the number of AI-generated posts each month
Hours saved per proposal, proposals submitted per quarter, win rate and report turnaround time
quiz.x: The module's indicators measure outcomes of adoption (hours saved, proposals submitted, win rate, turnaround), measured before and after. Account counts and training sessions measure activity, not results.

quiz.q: A junior officer at a Kampala NGO has used AI for every theory of change she has produced in two years. Her manager notices she cannot explain why one AI draft's causal logic is weak. Which risk is this?
opts: Homogenised voice, because her theories of change now sound like those of every other NGO
Dependency and deskilling, as she cannot judge quality in work she never learned to do herself
Data exposure, because programme designs were entered into a tool outside organisational control
Fabrication, because the AI is inventing causal pathways that have no basis in field evidence
quiz.x: Deskilling means staff who never learn a skill cannot judge whether AI did it well. Fabrication is the runner-up, but the problem described is her inability to evaluate, not invented content.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian women's rights NGO receives 4,000 WhatsApp feedback messages in Pidgin, French and Fulfulde and analyses them by theme within a week using AI. Which adoption stage does this illustrate?
opts: Stage 4, strategic advantage, because it does something that was previously impossible at scale
Stage 3, integrated systems, because the messaging platform's data is connected to the AI tool at all
Stage 2, shared workflows, because it relies on a reusable prompt and a standard codebook
Stage 1, individual productivity, because one staff member could run the analysis on a laptop
quiz.x: The module's Stage 4 example is analysing thousands of beneficiary messages in local languages within days, something previously impossible. Stage 3 concerns connecting systems with controls, not the new capability itself.

quiz.q: Mapping its value chain, an NGO lists: drafting donor updates, deciding which households qualify for cash transfers, translating training guides, and summarising meeting notes. Where should AI involvement be most limited?
opts: Translating training guides, because quality in local languages is lower than in English in practice
Deciding household eligibility, since it affects beneficiaries and needs verified local facts
Summarising meeting notes, because summaries may omit decisions that staff later need
Drafting donor updates, because donors may object to AI-written correspondence about results
quiz.x: AI is weakest and riskiest where decisions affect beneficiaries' eligibility or safety and depend on verified facts about real people. Translation is a real caution but is reviewable; eligibility decisions are high stakes.

facts.t: AI drafts the first 70%; humans invest the 30% that matters.
facts.more: Facts, figures, local context, donor nuance and ethics are the human 30%. NGOs that reverse the ratio end up submitting invented statistics.

facts.t: The adoption ladder: individual, shared workflows, integrated systems, strategic advantage.
facts.more: The most common failure is skipping stages, especially connecting AI to data before data governance exists.

facts.t: The NGO value chain: resource mobilisation, design, delivery, MEL, communications, operations.
facts.more: AI is strongest where work is text-heavy, repetitive and reviewable. It is weakest where work needs local trust or affects beneficiaries' safety or eligibility.

facts.t: Apply a theory of change to your own AI adoption.
facts.more: If staff get training, safe tools and templates, then drafting time falls, so more time goes to the field. Measure hours per proposal and win rate before and after.

modules.d: From donor research to a compliant, compelling proposal — with AI doing the heavy lifting and humans owning the truth.
modules.body:
Why proposals are won or lost before writing begins

Experienced fundraisers know that most rejected proposals fail on fit, not prose: the organisation applied for something outside the donor's priorities, geography or eligibility, or misread what the donor wanted to fund. The proposal engine therefore starts with a go/no-go decision, not a draft.

Step 1 — Donor intelligence and go/no-go

Read the call, the donor's strategy and their recently funded projects. Use AI to summarise long calls into a structured brief: objectives, eligible applicants, geographic focus, funding range, duration, co-financing requirements, mandatory annexes, evaluation criteria and their weights, and deadlines. Then decide honestly: Do we meet every eligibility criterion? Do we have relevant track record and evidence? Do we have partners if required? Can we deliver at this budget? Is the effort justified by our realistic chance? Applying to everything burns staff and lowers quality.

Step 2 — The problem and theory of change

Strong proposals begin with a precise problem analysis. A problem tree places the core problem in the trunk, its causes as roots and its effects as branches; turning it upside down — causes into objectives — produces the objective tree. The theory of change then explains how activities lead to outputs, outcomes and impact, and makes assumptions explicit. AI is useful for brainstorming causes and structuring the logic, but the evidence for each cause must come from real data: baseline surveys, government statistics, peer-reviewed studies, your own programme results.

Step 3 — The logframe

The logical framework summarises the design in a matrix: the hierarchy of objectives (goal, outcomes, outputs, activities), indicators for each level, means of verification, and assumptions. Indicators should be SMART and include baselines and targets. A frequent reviewer criticism is indicators that measure activity ("number of trainings held") at outcome level, where change in behaviour or condition ("percentage of trained farmers adopting improved storage") is required.

Reviewer's eye. Score your own draft against the published evaluation grid before submitting. If relevance carries 30 points and your relevance section is half a page of generic context, you are leaving points on the table. AI is excellent at mapping a draft against the criteria and flagging weak sections — ask it to act as a strict reviewer.

Step 4 — Drafting with AI, section by section

Feed the AI your structured inputs — donor brief, problem analysis, theory of change, logframe, organisational profile, relevant past results — and draft one section at a time. Specify the word limit, the evaluation criterion the section answers, the tone and the evidence to use. Never ask for "a full proposal" in one prompt; quality collapses and fabrication rises.

Step 5 — Budget and budget narrative

The budget must follow the logframe: every major activity costed, every cost justified, and consistent with the donor's eligible-cost rules and indirect-cost rate. AI can draft the budget narrative and check arithmetic consistency between narrative and spreadsheet, but unit costs must come from real quotations, salary scales and past expenditure. Mismatches between the narrative and the budget are a classic reason for rejection.

Step 6 — Compliance, review and the content library

Build a compliance checklist from the call: formats, page limits, annexes, signatures, registration documents, audited accounts. Have someone who did not write the proposal review it against the evaluation grid. After submission, store reusable sections — organisational profile, capacity statements, safeguarding policy summaries, past results with verified figures — in a content library. Over time the library, combined with AI drafting, cuts proposal time dramatically while keeping facts accurate.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my proposal engine. Step 1: I will paste a call for proposals; produce a structured donor brief and a go/no-go checklist. Step 2: help me build a problem tree and theory of change with explicit assumptions. Step 3: draft a logframe with SMART outcome indicators, baselines, targets and means of verification. Step 4: act as a strict reviewer and score my draft against the call's evaluation criteria, listing the weakest sections. Never invent statistics — mark any figure I must supply as [DATA NEEDED].

📚 Glossary

  • Go/no-go: the decision whether a call is worth applying for
  • Problem tree: causes (roots), core problem (trunk) and effects (branches)
  • Logframe: matrix of objectives, indicators, means of verification and assumptions
  • Means of verification: the source that will prove an indicator
  • Content library: verified, reusable proposal sections

📖 References

  • European Commission — Project Cycle Management Guidelines.
  • BOND — Logframe and theory of change guidance.
  • Funds for NGOs — proposal writing resources.
  • OECD-DAC — Evaluation criteria.

quiz.q: A Yaounde NGO finds an EU call on climate resilience. It has no work in the eligible regions, no required local partner and a budget floor triple its annual turnover. The team is keen to apply. What is the right step?
opts: Apply as lead and recruit a partner after the award to satisfy the call's partnership condition
Draft a strong concept note anyway, since persuasive writing can compensate for weaker eligibility
Ask AI to adapt last year's proposal quickly so that the cost of applying stays low for the team
Make a no-go decision and invest the effort in calls that fit the organisation's track record
quiz.x: Most proposals fail on fit, not prose; an honest go/no-go comes first. Promising partners after the award misreads eligibility, and a cheap recycled bid still burns staff time and quality.

quiz.q: A grants officer pastes a 60-page World Bank call into an AI assistant before deciding whether to bid. Which output request is most useful at this stage?
opts: A full first-draft proposal so the team can judge whether the effort is worth it before reading
A list of the donor's ten largest recent grants with the names of the organisations that won them
A structured brief of objectives, eligibility, geography, funding, annexes, criteria and deadlines
A summary of the call in plain French so that the board can read it at the next quarterly meeting
quiz.x: Step 1 uses AI to summarise long calls into a structured brief covering eligibility, funding, criteria weights and deadlines, which feeds the go/no-go. Recent grants help too, but they are one input, not the decision brief.

quiz.q: A problem tree for a Far North nutrition project shows 'chronic child malnutrition' as the core problem, with 'poor infant feeding practices' among the roots. Converting it into an objective tree, that root becomes:
opts: An effect on a branch, because feeding practices result from the malnutrition the project targets
A lower-level objective such as 'improved infant feeding practices among caregivers in target areas'
An assumption in the logframe, since caregiver behaviour lies outside the project's direct control here
An impact indicator, because changing feeding practices is the long-term goal of the intervention
quiz.x: Turning the problem tree upside down converts causes into objectives, so the root becomes a lower-level objective. Treating it as an assumption is the runner-up error: the project aims to change it, so it is an objective.

quiz.q: An agriculture project's logframe lists, at outcome level, 'number of storage trainings held: 40'. A reviewer flags it. Which replacement indicator fixes the problem?
opts: Average satisfaction score of participants on the post-training evaluation form, target 4 of 5 overall
Number of farmers attending storage trainings, disaggregated by sex and village, by year two
Number of training manuals on improved storage distributed to cooperatives in the target zone
Percentage of trained farmers using improved storage, from 10% baseline to 60% by end of project
quiz.x: Outcome indicators must measure change in behaviour or condition, with baseline and target. Attendance by sex is better disaggregated but still measures activity reach, not adoption.

quiz.q: A proposal's evaluation grid gives 30 of 100 points to relevance, but the draft's relevance section is half a page of generic national statistics. The deadline is in a week. What is the best use of AI now?
opts: Ask AI to shorten the other sections so that relevance becomes a larger share of the page limit
Ask AI to rewrite the whole proposal in a more persuasive tone that will appeal to the reviewers
Ask AI to act as a strict reviewer, score the draft against the grid and flag the weakest sections
Ask AI to expand the relevance section to three pages using additional national statistics it finds
quiz.x: Scoring the draft against the published grid with AI as a strict reviewer locates where points are lost. Expanding with AI-found statistics invites fabrication; the evidence must come from real data.

quiz.q: A grants manager in Lagos asks an AI assistant: 'Write our full 25-page proposal for the Gates call.' What does the module predict and recommend?
opts: Quality falls and fabrication rises; draft section by section with inputs, word limits and criteria
Good quality if the prompt is detailed enough; use one long prompt containing all the call text instead
Weak structure but accurate facts; ask a second AI tool to restructure the output into sections
Acceptable output for a first submission, followed by a section-by-section rewrite after feedback
quiz.x: The module says not to request a full proposal in one prompt: quality collapses and fabrication rises. Feed structured inputs and draft one section at a time with word limit, criterion, tone and evidence.

quiz.q: A budget narrative states that 12 community health workers will be paid 60,000 FCFA a month for 24 months, but the spreadsheet line shows 15,120,000 FCFA. What should the reviewer conclude?
opts: There is a mismatch: the narrative implies 17,280,000 FCFA, so one document must be corrected
The difference is likely indirect costs, which are normally added to salary lines in the budget
The figures match, since 12 workers at 60,000 FCFA for 24 months comes to 15,120,000 FCFA
There is a mismatch: the narrative implies 14,400,000 FCFA, so the spreadsheet line is too high
quiz.x: 12 x 60,000 x 24 = 17,280,000 FCFA, so narrative and spreadsheet disagree; such mismatches are a classic rejection reason. 15,120,000 would be 21 months; indirect costs follow the donor's rate and are not hidden in salary lines.

quiz.q: A small NGO's AI-drafted budget uses unit costs of 25 USD per training participant per day 'based on typical regional rates'. Where should those unit costs come from?
opts: From the AI's estimate, cross-checked with a second AI tool to confirm it is within a sensible range
From the donor's published average costs for similar projects across all countries in the region
From real quotations, the organisation's salary scales and its past expenditure on similar trainings
From a peer NGO's successful budget for a comparable training programme in a neighbouring country recently
quiz.x: Unit costs must come from real quotations, salary scales and past expenditure; AI may draft the narrative and check arithmetic. A peer's budget is a defensible reference but reflects their context and prices, not yours.

quiz.q: After winning a USAID-funded subaward, an NGO in Dakar wants future proposals to be faster without losing accuracy. Which practice does the module recommend?
opts: Save the winning proposal as a template and ask AI to replace donor names for each new call
Train a custom AI model on all past proposals so it can produce new ones without staff input
Hire a freelance writer to adapt the winning text quickly for each new opportunity that appears
Keep a content library of verified sections such as organisational profile and past results
quiz.x: A content library of reusable, verified sections combined with AI drafting cuts proposal time while keeping facts accurate. Swapping donor names in an old proposal ignores fit and each call's criteria.

quiz.q: The person who wrote a 40-page proposal also checked it against the compliance list the night before submission. A missing audited-accounts annex was not caught. Which practice would most likely have prevented this?
opts: Asking AI to confirm that the proposal reads well and meets the page limits for each section
A compliance checklist built from the call, checked by someone who did not write the proposal
Submitting a week earlier so that the donor can point out missing annexes before the deadline
Asking the writer to re-read the proposal twice more on the morning of the submission deadline
quiz.x: The module recommends a compliance checklist from the call and a review by someone who did not write it; authors miss their own gaps. Earlier submission helps timing but donors do not usually return incomplete bids for fixing.

facts.t: Most rejected proposals fail on donor fit, not writing quality.
facts.more: Priorities, geography and eligibility decide first. That's why the engine starts with a go/no-go decision.

facts.t: Logframe hierarchy: goal, outcomes, outputs, activities.
facts.more: Each level has indicators, means of verification and assumptions. Reviewers penalise activity counts placed at outcome level.

facts.t: In a problem tree, the core problem is the trunk, causes are roots, effects are branches.
facts.more: Turning causes into objectives gives you the objective tree. AI can brainstorm causes, but the evidence for each must come from real data.

facts.t: Indicators should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
facts.more: Each needs a baseline and a target. 'Percentage of trained farmers adopting improved storage' beats 'number of trainings held' at outcome level.

modules.d: Choosing tools by job-to-be-done, cost, data protection and field conditions — not by hype.
modules.body:
Start from jobs, not products

The AI tool market changes monthly; features and prices you read about today may be different next quarter. A durable approach is to define the jobs your organisation needs done, then evaluate tools against criteria. Always verify current features, pricing and data terms directly with the provider before committing.

The main tool categories

  • General AI assistants (for example ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot): drafting, summarising, translation, brainstorming, analysis of documents. The workhorse for most NGO staff. Key question: which plan keeps your data out of model training and offers organisational controls?
  • Productivity-suite AI built into Google Workspace or Microsoft 365: assistance inside documents, spreadsheets, email and meetings. Strong when your organisation already lives in that suite; nonprofit programmes may offer discounted or donated licences.
  • Data collection platforms such as KoboToolbox and ODK: offline mobile surveys widely used in humanitarian and development work, increasingly paired with AI for cleaning and analysing results.
  • Qualitative analysis tools: coding interviews and open-ended survey responses. General assistants can do much of this with careful prompting; specialist tools add audit trails and team coding.
  • Translation and transcription: speech-to-text and translation for interviews, community meetings and multilingual materials. Quality varies greatly by language; test with your actual languages and accents.
  • Donor and contact management (CRM): platforms such as Salesforce Nonprofit, CiviCRM or simpler tools, increasingly with AI features for segmentation and drafting.
  • Automation platforms such as Zapier or Make: connecting forms, sheets, email and messaging without code — for example, automatically acknowledging donations or routing feedback.
  • Design and communications: tools such as Canva for reports, social posts and infographics.
Nonprofit discounts are real but conditional. Programmes such as TechSoup and providers' own nonprofit offers can significantly reduce costs, usually requiring proof of registration and eligibility. Factor in the cost after any discount period ends.

Evaluation criteria that matter for NGOs

  1. Fit to the job: does it do the specific task well in your languages and formats?
  2. Data protection: where is data stored, is it used for training, can you sign a data-processing agreement, does it meet donor and national legal requirements?
  3. Field conditions: does it work offline or on low bandwidth, on basic Android phones, with intermittent power?
  4. Total cost of ownership: licences, training, integration, support, and cost after discounts or free tiers end.
  5. Ease of use: can staff with modest digital skills use it after short training?
  6. Interoperability: can it export data in standard formats so you are not locked in?
  7. Sustainability: will the provider and your budget support it beyond the current grant?

Running a fair pilot

Choose two or three candidate tools for one job. Define a realistic test using your own (non-sensitive or anonymised) material — a past report, a set of survey responses, an interview in a local language. Score each tool against the criteria with the staff who will use it. Run for two to four weeks, record time saved and quality, and decide. Avoid "pilot purgatory": set the decision date before starting.

A minimal stack for a small NGO

Many small organisations can achieve most of the benefit with four components: one general AI assistant on a plan with appropriate data protection, their existing productivity suite, an offline data collection tool, and a simple automation platform. Complexity can follow need.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my nonprofit technology advisor. Ask me about our size, budget, languages, connectivity, existing software and the three jobs we most need help with. For each job, suggest two or three tool categories and example tools, list the evaluation criteria that matter most for us, and design a two-week pilot with a scoring sheet. Remind me which features and prices I must verify directly with providers.

📚 Glossary

  • Job-to-be-done: the specific task a tool must accomplish
  • Total cost of ownership: all costs over the tool's life, not just the licence
  • Data-processing agreement: contract defining how a provider handles your data
  • Interoperability: ability to exchange data with other systems in standard formats
  • Pilot purgatory: endless pilots without a decision

📖 References

  • KoboToolbox and ODK documentation.

quiz.q: An NGO in Kinshasa reads a 2024 blog listing an AI tool's features and price, and wants to sign a two-year contract based on it. What does the module advise first?
opts: Choose the tool with the most features listed so the organisation is covered as needs grow
Verify current features, pricing and data terms directly with the provider before committing
Wait a year for the market to settle so that the NGO can choose a more mature, stable product
Sign quickly, since prices in the AI market tend to rise as tools gain more paying customers
quiz.x: The AI tool market changes monthly, so current features, prices and data terms must be checked with the provider. Waiting a year forgoes value; features-first ignores the jobs-to-be-done approach.

quiz.q: A humanitarian NGO needs enumerators to run household surveys in areas with no network for days at a time. Which tool category fits this job best?
opts: An offline mobile data collection platform such as KoboToolbox or ODK, synced when back online
A general AI assistant on a team plan, with enumerators sending answers by chat when they can again
A CRM platform with AI segmentation features so households can be grouped automatically
An automation platform that routes each survey response from a web form into a spreadsheet
quiz.x: KoboToolbox and ODK are offline mobile survey tools widely used in humanitarian work. A web form plus automation needs connectivity at the point of collection.

quiz.q: A rural NGO is offered donated licences for the office suite its staff already work in daily, and also looks at a separate AI writing tool. Which consideration best supports the built-in suite option?
opts: It is the most accurate translator for African languages because it is built by a large company
It replaces the need for an offline data collection tool because documents sync automatically
It removes the need for a data protection review since the vendor is a well-known global provider
It suits teams that spend their working hours inside it, and nonprofit pricing may be available
quiz.x: Productivity-suite AI is strong when the organisation already works in that suite, and nonprofit programmes may offer discounted or donated licences. Vendor size does not remove the need for a data review.

quiz.q: TechSoup offers an NGO a deep discount on software for the first year. The finance officer asks what else to factor in. What is the most important additional consideration?
opts: Whether the provider's founder has a personal connection to the NGO sector in the region
Whether the discounted licence includes a public listing of the NGO on the provider's website
The cost after the discount ends, plus training, integration and support across the grant period in full
The number of features unlocked by the discount compared with the provider's free tier
quiz.x: Nonprofit discounts are real but conditional; total cost of ownership includes licences after the discount, training, integration and support. Feature counts do not address sustainability.

quiz.q: An NGO tests three transcription tools on clean English audio from a head-office meeting and picks the best. It then uses the tool for Ewondo focus groups. What flaw does the module highlight?
opts: The test should have been scored by the IT team rather than by the staff who will use it
The test ran too long; a single afternoon is normally enough for a transcription comparison
The test used too few tools; at least five should be compared for a decision of this importance
The test did not use the actual languages and accents, where quality can vary greatly
quiz.x: Translation and transcription quality varies greatly by language; tests must use your actual languages, accents and material. Fair pilots are scored with the staff who will use the tool, not IT alone.

quiz.q: A Ugandan NGO has piloted two AI tools for 'a few months' with no end date, and staff keep asking which one to use. What practice would have avoided this?
opts: Setting the decision date before the pilot starts, with two to four weeks of scored testing
Extending the pilot until each tool has been used for a full annual reporting cycle
Choosing the cheaper tool at the start so that the pilot carries less financial risk in full
Running the pilot with every staff member so the final decision has wider acceptance
quiz.x: To avoid 'pilot purgatory', set the decision date before starting and run two to four weeks of scored testing. Wider participation helps buy-in but does not force a decision.

quiz.q: A 12-person NGO in Lome wants most of AI's benefit with minimal complexity. Which combination matches the module's minimal stack?
opts: An integrated enterprise platform connecting finance, HR, CRM and surveys with AI across all of them
A CRM with AI features, a specialist qualitative analysis tool, a design tool and a custom chatbot for donors
A general AI assistant with data protection, their productivity suite, offline data collection and simple automation
A free consumer chatbot for all staff, a paid transcription service and a satellite imagery platform
quiz.x: The module's minimal stack is a general assistant on a plan with data protection, the existing productivity suite, an offline data collection tool and a simple automation platform; complexity follows need.

quiz.q: An NGO wants every online donation to trigger an automatic thank-you email and a row in a donor spreadsheet, without hiring a developer. Which tool category fits?
opts: A general AI assistant asked to draft a thank-you template that staff send by hand each week for review
An automation platform such as Zapier or Make, connecting the donation form, sheet and email
A design tool that produces branded thank-you cards which staff can post on social media
A qualitative analysis tool that codes donor messages and flags those that need a reply
quiz.x: Automation platforms such as Zapier or Make connect forms, sheets and email without code, for example automatically acknowledging donations. A drafted template still leaves manual sending.

quiz.q: Two AI assistants score equally on drafting quality for an NGO's French reports. One stores information in a region acceptable to its EU donor and offers a signed processing agreement; the other does not. Which criterion decides?
opts: Data protection, including storage location, training use and a data-processing agreement
Ease of use, since staff with modest digital skills need to adopt the tool quickly for staff
Fit to the job, since the tool must handle French well for the organisation's donors
Interoperability, since exporting reports in standard formats avoids future lock-in
quiz.x: With fit to the job equal, data protection (storage, training use, DPA, donor and legal requirements) becomes the deciding criterion. Fit to the job was already tied, so it cannot break the tie.

quiz.q: An NGO's preferred AI tool cannot export its records in any common file type, and moving to another tool would mean re-entering two years of work by hand. Which evaluation criterion was neglected?
opts: Field conditions, because the tool has to function on basic Android phones and low bandwidth
Total cost of ownership, because licence fees will rise as the organisation adds more users
Sustainability, because the provider may not survive beyond the current funding period
Interoperability, because data that cannot be exported in standard formats creates lock-in
quiz.x: Interoperability asks whether data exports in standard formats so you are not locked in. Sustainability is related but concerns whether provider and budget last, not data portability.

facts.t: KoboToolbox was developed at the Harvard Humanitarian Initiative.
facts.more: Built on Open Data Kit, it is widely used for offline mobile surveys in humanitarian and development work. Many NGOs in Central Africa already use it.

facts.t: Total cost of ownership: licences, training, integration, support, and the price after discounts end.
facts.more: A free tier or a one-year donation can turn into a budget shock in year two. Plan beyond the current grant.

facts.t: A minimal small-NGO stack: one AI assistant, your productivity suite, offline data collection, simple automation.
facts.more: Most of the benefit comes from these four. Add complexity only when a real need appears.

facts.t: Length of a fair tool pilot with a fixed decision date.
facts.more: Two or three candidates, your own anonymised material, scored by the staff who will use it. Set the date up front to avoid pilot purgatory.

modules.d: Faster, more rigorous monitoring, evaluation and reporting — without compromising evidence.
modules.body:
M&E is where credibility is built or lost

Donors increasingly fund organisations that can show results with evidence. Yet in many NGOs, monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning (MEAL) is understaffed, and reporting season becomes a scramble to compile numbers and stories. AI can transform the speed of this work — but only if the underlying data is sound. AI cannot create evidence; it can only help you process and present it.

The M&E framework

A robust framework links each logframe indicator to a definition, data source, collection method, frequency, responsible person, baseline and target, and disaggregation (sex, age, disability, location). The OECD-DAC evaluation criteria — relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability — structure most evaluations and many donor reports. Knowing which criterion each section answers keeps reports focused.

Where AI accelerates MEAL

  • Tool design: drafting survey questions aligned to indicators, checking for leading or double-barrelled questions, and translating instruments — always back-translated and piloted.
  • Data cleaning: generating formulas or scripts to detect duplicates, outliers, impossible values and inconsistent dates.
  • Quantitative analysis: writing spreadsheet formulas, pivot tables or simple analysis code; explaining statistical results in plain language.
  • Qualitative analysis: coding open-ended responses, focus-group transcripts and feedback messages into themes — the biggest time-saver for many teams.
  • Reporting: drafting narrative sections from structured results, tailoring the same results for different donors, and creating summaries and infographics.
Qualitative coding with integrity. Give the AI a clear codebook (theme definitions and examples), ask it to code a sample, then have a human code the same sample and compare. Refine the codebook until agreement is high, then code the full set and spot-check. Always ask for supporting quotes for each theme, and verify that the quotes exist in the source. Report how the analysis was done.

Verification: the non-negotiable step

Every number in a donor report must trace back to a data source you can show an auditor. A practical rule: the AI may describe numbers you give it, but never produce numbers on its own. Reconcile totals across sections (people reached by sex should sum to the total), check percentages against their denominators, and compare with previous reports for unexplained jumps. Many donor audits find discrepancies between narrative and financial reports — a reconciliation step before submission prevents this.

Telling the story honestly

Donors value honest reporting of what did not work as much as successes; it signals learning. AI can help structure a report around results, challenges, adaptations and lessons learned. Stories of change should be real, with informed consent from the people featured, and should not be embellished. A composite or illustrative story must be labelled as such.

From reporting to learning

The purpose of M&E is not the report — it is better programmes. Use AI to make learning faster: summarising monthly feedback trends for programme meetings, comparing results across sites, and drafting short learning briefs. Organisations that close the loop between data and decisions get better results and stronger donor relationships.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my MEAL analyst. Step 1: I will paste anonymised open-ended survey responses and a draft codebook. Code a sample of 30 responses, show me your coding with supporting quotes, and suggest codebook refinements. Step 2: given my indicator results table, check internal consistency (totals, disaggregation, percentages). Step 3: draft a donor report section structured around results, challenges, adaptations and lessons learned — using only the numbers I provide and flagging any gaps.

📚 Glossary

  • MEAL: monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning
  • Disaggregation: breaking data down by sex, age, disability, location etc.
  • Codebook: defined themes with rules and examples for qualitative coding
  • Back-translation: translating a tool back to the original language to check accuracy
  • OECD-DAC criteria: relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability

📖 References

  • OECD-DAC (2019). Better Criteria for Better Evaluation.
  • Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology.
  • Better Evaluation — methods and approaches.
  • IFRC — Project/programme monitoring and evaluation guide.

quiz.q: An NGO's donor report states 1,240 people were reached: 610 women and 590 men. The M&E officer asks AI to 'polish the results section'. What should happen before the report is sent?
opts: Let the AI adjust the sex-disaggregated figures so that they are consistent with the total
Reconcile the figures against source data, since 610 plus 590 is 1,200, not 1,240 as reported
Accept the figures, as small gaps of this size are normal in programme monitoring data
Report the total as 'over 1,200' so that the discrepancy is no longer visible to the donor overall
quiz.x: Disaggregated figures should sum to the total; 610 + 590 = 1,200, a 40-person gap. AI may describe numbers it is given but must not produce or adjust them; the source data must be reconciled.

quiz.q: An M&E officer in Abuja asks AI to code 800 open-ended survey responses into themes. Which process best preserves integrity?
opts: Have AI code all responses, then ask a second AI tool to verify the coding for consistency in full
Code a sample by hand and let AI code the remainder without a codebook to avoid human bias
Provide a codebook, compare AI and human coding on a sample, refine, then code all and spot-check
Let AI create themes freely, then accept the themes that appear most often in the output
quiz.x: The module's method: clear codebook, AI and human code the same sample, compare and refine until agreement is high, then code the full set and spot-check, with verified quotes. Two AIs checking each other do not provide human validation.

quiz.q: An AI-coded thematic analysis lists the quote 'The water point changed our lives' under the theme 'access'. Before using it in a report, the officer should:
opts: Keep it if it reflects the general theme, even if the exact wording is not found
Lightly edit the quote for grammar so that it reads well in the donor's language
Check that the quote exists in the source transcripts and was given with consent
Replace it with a quote from staff field notes, which are easier to verify in time
quiz.x: AI can invent quotes; each supporting quote must be verified against the source, and stories need informed consent. A 'representative' quote not found in the data is fabrication.

quiz.q: An evaluation report for an EU-funded project has a section on whether results will last after funding ends. Which OECD-DAC criterion does this section answer?
opts: Effectiveness, because it concerns whether the project achieved its intended outcomes
Coherence, because it concerns how the project fits with other interventions in the area
Impact, because it concerns the long-term changes produced by the intervention in the area
Sustainability, because it concerns whether the benefits continue after funding stops
quiz.x: Sustainability asks whether benefits continue after funding ends. Impact, the runner-up, concerns the broader higher-level effects, positive or negative, not their durability.

quiz.q: An M&E plan lists an indicator with only a name and a target. The donor asks for a stronger framework. Which addition set matches the module?
opts: A narrative paragraph explaining why the indicator matters to beneficiaries and the donor in turn
Definition, data source, method, frequency, responsible person, baseline and disaggregation
Three alternative indicators so the team can report whichever shows the best results
An infographic template and an AI prompt for generating the quarterly reporting narrative
quiz.x: A robust framework links each indicator to definition, source, method, frequency, responsibility, baseline, target and disaggregation by sex, age, disability and location.

quiz.q: A draft survey for a Togo project asks: 'How satisfied are you with the training and the materials?' An AI review flags it. Why?
opts: It is double-barrelled, combining two items so the answer cannot be attributed to either
It lacks a disability disaggregation, so it cannot be used for inclusive reporting
It is too long for a mobile survey and should be cut to fewer than ten words for enumerators
It is a leading question, because it assumes the respondent was satisfied with the training
quiz.x: Asking about training and materials in one item is double-barrelled. 'How satisfied' presumes some satisfaction, which is a weaker concern than the two-in-one problem.

quiz.q: An NGO's annual report includes a moving story about 'Mama Ngozi', which staff built by combining three real beneficiaries' experiences. How should it be presented?
opts: Labelled clearly as a composite or illustrative story, with consent from the people drawn on
Removed from the report, because composite stories are not accepted in most donor reporting
With a changed name and photo of a different beneficiary so that privacy is better protected in practice
As a real person's story, since each detail is true and the story is more powerful that way
quiz.x: Composite or illustrative stories must be labelled as such, and stories require informed consent. Presenting a composite as a real person misleads donors; using a different person's photo misrepresents them.

quiz.q: Mid-term data shows a savings-group project missed its loan repayment target by 30% in two of five sites. The communications officer wants to leave it out of the donor report. What does the module recommend?
opts: Report it as a footnote under the results table so that the main narrative stays positive
Report the three successful sites and describe the other two as still in progress
Leave it out until the final report, when the sites may have recovered and the data improved
Report it honestly with the challenges, adaptations and lessons, since donors value learning
quiz.x: Donors value honest reporting of what did not work as it signals learning; reports should cover results, challenges, adaptations and lessons. Burying it in a footnote is the softer version of the same evasion.

quiz.q: Last year a project reported 2,000 households reached; this year's AI-drafted report says 6,500 with the same budget and staff. What step should come before submission?
opts: Average the two years and report 4,250 households to present a more realistic trend
Compare with previous reports and trace the figure to source data to explain the jump
Accept it, since AI drafting tools are generally accurate when summarising tabulated data
Ask the AI to explain the increase and include its explanation in the report narrative
quiz.x: Comparing with previous reports for unexplained jumps and tracing every number to a source is the verification rule. An AI explanation is not evidence.

quiz.q: A programme manager says: 'Our M&E is fine, we submit every report on time.' Which practice would most improve M&E by the module's standard?
opts: Switching to a more advanced statistical package that can process larger datasets faster
Adding more indicators to each logframe level to demonstrate thoroughness to reviewers
Using AI to summarise monthly feedback trends for programme meetings and adapt activities
Producing longer reports with more charts so that donors see the volume of data collected for them
quiz.x: The purpose of M&E is better programmes; closing the loop between data and decisions, for example monthly feedback summaries for programme meetings, is what the module emphasises over the report itself.

facts.t: OECD-DAC evaluation criteria: relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability.
facts.more: Coherence was added in the 2019 revision. Knowing which criterion each report section answers keeps reports focused.

facts.t: Braun & Clarke's thematic analysis process for qualitative data.
facts.more: Familiarise, generate codes, search for themes, review themes, define and name them, write up. AI can speed up coding, but a human-tested codebook keeps it honest.

facts.t: How many numbers the AI may produce on its own in a donor report.
facts.more: AI may describe numbers you give it. Every figure must trace to a source you can show an auditor.

facts.t: Translate a survey back into the original language to check accuracy.
facts.more: Combined with piloting, it catches meaning shifts that AI translation introduces, especially in less-resourced African languages.

plaibox.intro: You are the MEAL officer of a Douala NGO. The donor report is due Friday. Scoring: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: The AI's draft says '1,200 youth found jobs'. Your tracker shows 840 confirmed placements.

Every number must trace to your data. Report the verified figure.
Report 'over 1,000' as a compromise between the figures

steps.s: AI coding of 600 feedback messages shows 'satisfaction' as the top theme.
o: Accept it: AI coding is consistent across all responses
Without human validation, you don't know whether the codebook is working.
Hand-code a sample of 50, compare, and refine the codebook
This is the integrity process for AI qualitative coding.
Re-run the AI with a more detailed, different prompt

steps.s: One district missed its target because of insecurity on access roads.
o: Report it with the adaptation you made and the lesson
Honest reporting of challenges signals learning, which donors value.
Leave the district out of the totals to keep data clean
Hiding results is misreporting.
Mention it briefly in an annex at the end of the report
Transparent, but it buries a learning point donors value.

steps.s: Communications wants a powerful beneficiary story by tomorrow.
o: Use a real story with consent, or label a composite clearly
Real, consented, or clearly labelled. That is the standard.
Let AI write a moving story with an invented name
Presented as real, it's fabrication.
Use a real story but skip the consent step this once
