plaibox.win: Excellent. Verified numbers, validated coding, honest challenges and consented stories.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the verification rule: AI never produces numbers, and every story needs consent.

modules.d: Low-bandwidth workflows, local languages, consent and doing no harm with beneficiary data.
modules.body:
Designing for the field, not the head office

Many AI demonstrations assume fast internet, a laptop and English. Field reality is often different: intermittent connectivity, shared or basic Android phones, expensive data, unreliable power, and communities speaking several local languages. AI strategies designed for head office routinely fail in the field. Design for the hardest context first and you will usually serve everyone.

Low-bandwidth and offline workflows

  • Collect offline, process centrally: field teams use offline survey tools; AI analysis happens at the office once data syncs.
  • Lightweight channels: SMS, USSD and WhatsApp reach far more people than apps or web portals. Voice notes are often more inclusive than text for low-literacy communities.
  • Prepare before travel: download materials, translated guides and checklists while connected.
  • Batch, not stream: send data and AI requests in batches when connectivity allows, rather than relying on constant connection.
  • Cost awareness: data bundles cost staff and communities money; compress files and avoid heavy media where possible.

Local languages and inclusion

AI performs best in widely represented languages and much worse in many African languages, accents and code-switched speech. Never assume an AI translation of community materials is correct. Work with native speakers to review, test materials with community members, and be honest in reports about translation limitations. Inclusive design also considers literacy, disability, gender and age — who can actually access and use a digital channel.

Do no harm. The humanitarian principle of "do no harm" applies to data. A list of people who received assistance, their location, ethnicity, health status or protection concerns could put them at risk if leaked, seized or misused. Treat beneficiary data as you would treat the people themselves.

Responsible data principles

  1. Purpose limitation: collect only what you need for a defined purpose, and use it only for that purpose.
  2. Data minimisation: if you do not need names to analyse feedback, remove them before analysis.
  3. Informed consent: people understand what data is collected, why, who will see it and how long it is kept — in their language, and with a genuine option to refuse without losing assistance.
  4. Security: encryption, access controls, secure devices and clear retention and deletion rules.
  5. Accountability: named data owners, documented processes and breach response plans.

AI-specific data rules

Staff must know clearly what may and may not be entered into AI tools. A simple three-tier rule works for many NGOs. Green: public or fully anonymised information — may be used with approved tools. Amber: internal, non-personal information — only with approved organisational tools under appropriate data terms. Red: personal or sensitive beneficiary data, protection cases, health information, staff records — never entered into general AI tools; processed only in approved, secured systems with legal basis. Anonymisation must be real: a combination of village, age, sex and disability can identify a person even without a name.

Law and donor requirements

Data protection laws increasingly apply across Africa and beyond — including the EU GDPR when working with European donors or data, and national laws such as Cameroon's recent personal data protection legislation. Donors such as the EU, UN agencies and many foundations also impose data protection and safeguarding clauses. Know the rules that apply to your operations, and seek legal advice when processing sensitive data at scale.

Safeguarding and AI

Safeguarding policies protect beneficiaries, especially children and vulnerable adults. AI introduces new considerations: images of beneficiaries used in AI tools, AI-generated images that misrepresent communities, and chatbots interacting with vulnerable people without human oversight. Include AI explicitly in your safeguarding policy.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my responsible-data advisor. Ask me what data my programmes collect, from whom, through which channels and in which languages. Then classify each data type as green, amber or red for AI use, design a low-bandwidth field workflow for one programme, draft a plain-language consent statement for community members, and list the anonymisation steps needed before any AI analysis.

📚 Glossary

  • Do no harm: ensuring interventions, including data use, do not put people at risk
  • Data minimisation: collecting and using only the data needed
  • Informed consent: voluntary agreement based on understanding of data use
  • Re-identification: identifying a person from combined non-name data
  • Safeguarding: protecting people, especially the vulnerable, from harm

📖 References

  • ICRC — Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action.
  • The Engine Room — Responsible Data resources.
  • Sphere Handbook — Protection Principles.
  • European Union — General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
  • Republic of Cameroon — personal data protection legislation (verify current text).

quiz.q: An NGO plans a smartphone app for farmers in rural Adamawa, where many use shared basic phones and data is expensive. Which channel choice best fits the module's guidance?
opts: A web portal optimised for laptops in town, which farmers can visit on market days
A rich mobile app with video tutorials, since engaging content improves farmer retention
An app with offline mode but large downloads, so that content can be cached in advance
SMS, USSD, WhatsApp or voice notes, which reach more people and suit low-literacy users
quiz.x: Lightweight channels such as SMS, USSD and WhatsApp reach far more people, and voice notes are more inclusive for low-literacy users. An offline app with big downloads still assumes smartphones and costly data.

quiz.q: An AI tool translates a cholera prevention leaflet into Hausa for a Nigerian community. The team lead is satisfied because 'the AI is very good'. What is the right next step?
opts: Have native speakers review it and test it with community members before distribution
Distribute the leaflet now, then correct errors if community members report problems later
Translate it with a second AI tool and keep whichever version reads more naturally
Add an English version on the reverse so that readers can check the meaning themselves
quiz.x: AI performs much worse in many African languages; native speakers must review and materials should be tested with the community. A second AI tool adds no native-speaker verification.

quiz.q: An NGO removes names from a feedback dataset before AI analysis but keeps village, age, sex and disability status. A small village has one 34-year-old woman with a disability. What is the problem?
opts: None, because removing names is the accepted standard for anonymising beneficiary data
The combination of fields can still identify her, so the data is not really anonymised
Age should be rounded to the nearest year, after which the data can be used freely
Disability status is not personal data, so keeping it raises no data protection concern
quiz.x: Anonymisation must be real: a combination of village, age, sex and disability can identify a person without a name. Rounding age to the nearest year changes nothing in this case.

quiz.q: Under a green/amber/red data rule, how should an NGO classify its internal draft strategy (no personal data) and a list of GBV survivors' case notes?
opts: Strategy amber, case notes amber, provided the case notes are anonymised before use
Strategy green, case notes amber, as both may go into approved tools with a staff review before use
Strategy amber, case notes red: internal material in approved tools, case notes kept out of AI
Strategy red, case notes red, since any internal document must stay out of AI tools
quiz.x: Amber is internal, non-personal information for approved organisational tools; red is sensitive beneficiary and protection data, which never goes into general AI tools. Anonymising protection cases is risky and does not downgrade them to amber by default.

quiz.q: A food distribution NGO's consent form is in English, read quickly to recipients in a queue, and implies aid depends on signing. Which element of informed consent is most clearly missing?
opts: Understanding in their language with a genuine option to refuse without losing assistance
A statement of the legal basis under the national data protection law that applies fully
A signature from a community leader confirming that the process was properly followed
A record of the time and location of consent for audit purposes by the donor
quiz.x: Informed consent means people understand what is collected, why and for how long, in their language, with a genuine option to refuse without losing assistance. A leader's signature does not supply individual understanding.

quiz.q: A field team in eastern DRC has connectivity for an hour each evening at the base. They want AI help analysing daily survey data. Which workflow matches the module?
opts: Have enumerators type responses into a chatbot during interviews for instant summaries
Collect offline during the day, sync in batches, then run AI analysis centrally once data arrives
Stream each survey to the AI tool in real time using satellite data as interviews happen each day
Delay data collection until a reliable connection is installed at each survey location
quiz.x: Collect offline, process centrally, and batch rather than stream are the module's low-bandwidth principles. Waiting for connectivity delays the work for no gain.

quiz.q: An NGO working with an EU donor in Cameroon processes health information on thousands of beneficiaries. Which legal stance is most appropriate?
opts: Wait until regulators publish detailed guidance before adjusting the organisation's practices
Apply the donor's contract clauses, and treat national law as relevant to government bodies
Identify the applicable laws, including GDPR and Cameroon's data law, and seek legal advice at scale
Rely on the AI provider's terms of service, since the provider is responsible for data compliance
quiz.x: Data protection laws such as GDPR and Cameroon's recent personal data protection law, plus donor clauses, may all apply; seek legal advice for sensitive data at scale. Donor clauses are necessary but not the whole picture.

quiz.q: A communications officer generates an AI image of 'a typical malnourished village child' for a fundraising appeal. Which concern does the module raise?
opts: AI images are lower resolution than photographs and look unprofessional in printed materials
It may breach the copyright of the photographer whose work the AI tool was trained on
It will reduce donations because donors prefer to see real photographs of beneficiaries
It may misrepresent communities and should be covered by the organisation's safeguarding policy
quiz.x: AI-generated images that misrepresent communities are a safeguarding consideration, and AI should be included explicitly in safeguarding policy. Copyright is a real question but not the module's point here.

quiz.q: A protection NGO wants a chatbot to answer questions from vulnerable adolescents on WhatsApp at night when staff are offline. What is the main safeguarding issue?
opts: WhatsApp groups are harder to moderate than SMS channels for large numbers of users
Night-time messaging may cost adolescents more for data than daytime messaging does
Vulnerable people interacting with a chatbot without human oversight raises safeguarding risk
Chatbots in local languages have higher error rates than those in widely spoken languages yet
quiz.x: Chatbots interacting with vulnerable people without human oversight is a named safeguarding risk. Language error rates matter too, but the core issue is unsupervised contact with vulnerable users.

quiz.q: A cash-transfer NGO wants to collect beneficiaries' religion and ethnicity 'in case it is useful later' for AI analysis. Which principle does this breach?
opts: Accountability, because no named data owner has been appointed for the new fields
Security, because the fields would need encryption under most national laws
Informed consent, because beneficiaries cannot be asked about religion at all
Purpose limitation and data minimisation: collect what a defined purpose needs
quiz.x: Collecting data 'in case' violates purpose limitation and data minimisation; under do no harm, such fields could also put people at risk. Security and ownership matter but come after deciding whether to collect at all.

facts.t: Green, amber, red: a simple rule for what may go into AI tools.
facts.more: Green = public or truly anonymised. Amber = internal, non-personal, approved tools only. Red = personal or sensitive beneficiary data, never in general AI tools.

facts.t: Maximum GDPR fine tier: up to 4% of global annual turnover or €20 million, whichever is higher.
facts.more: It applies when you process EU-linked personal data, for example with European donors or partners. Donor contracts often import similar duties.

facts.t: Protection Principles in the Sphere Handbook.
facts.more: The first is to enhance people's safety, dignity and rights and avoid exposing them to further harm, which applies directly to how you handle their data.

facts.t: Combined details can identify a person with no name attached.
facts.more: Re-identification is easy in small communities. Real anonymisation removes or generalises these combinations before AI analysis.

labs.title: Green, amber or red?
labs.intro: Classify each data item for AI use under the three-tier rule.
items: Published annual report
Fully anonymised, aggregated survey percentages
Draft internal budget for next year
Staff meeting notes with no personal details
List of GBV survivors receiving support
HIV status of programme participants
Feedback with village, age, sex and disability left in
Staff payroll and appraisal records
labs.tip: When in doubt, it's red. Anonymisation must be real, not just removing names.

labs.title: Spot the problems in this field data plan
labs.intro: A coordinator's AI-assisted plan for collecting feedback in remote Northwest villages. Tap the risky parts.
segments: Enumerators will use KoboToolbox offline on Android phones.
Data syncs at the field office each evening.
We will collect full names, phone numbers and ethnicity for all respondents just in case.
It breaks data minimisation and purpose limitation, and ethnicity is sensitive in an insecure context.
Consent will be explained in English only to keep it consistent.
Informed consent must be in a language people understand.
Respondents who refuse will be dropped from the food distribution list.
Consent isn't voluntary if refusing costs assistance.
Voice notes will be offered for respondents with low literacy.
Raw transcripts will be pasted into a free chatbot for analysis.
Personal beneficiary data is red tier and must not go into general AI tools.
Names are removed before analysis and devices are encrypted.
labs.tip: Minimise, consent genuinely in the right language, secure, and keep red data out of AI.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the protection-sensitive programme
plaibox.intro: You manage a programme for displaced families near Buea. Scoring: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: A donor asks for a beneficiary list with names and GPS points 'for verification'.
o: Send the full file by email; donors are trusted partners
Location data on displaced people could put them at risk if leaked or seized.
Offer aggregated data plus an on-site spot-check with safeguards
Meets the verification need while applying do no harm and minimisation.
Send names and villages but remove the GPS coordinates
Less risky, but still more personal data than the purpose needs.

steps.s: Staff want to analyse 2,000 WhatsApp feedback messages with AI.
o: Strip identifiers, then use the approved tool
Anonymise first, then use approved tools. That is the amber-to-green pathway.
Paste them as-is into a free chatbot for speed
Red-tier data in a general tool breaches consent and law.
Analyse only a sample of 200 messages by hand
Safe but slow. Proper anonymisation makes AI usable.

steps.s: The AI translation of your consent form into Pidgin reads oddly.
o: Use it anyway; it's close enough for people to understand
Consent must be understood. A bad translation invalidates it.
Switch to French for everyone, since most people read it
Consistent, but many participants won't fully understand.
Have native speakers revise it and test it with the community
Native review and testing make consent genuine.

steps.s: Comms proposes AI-generated images of 'displaced children' for a fundraising post.
o: Use them; no real child is exposed or identifiable
Avoids exposure, but it may misrepresent communities. Label it at minimum and follow the safeguarding policy.
Use consented, dignified real photos per policy, or none
Safeguarding covers AI imagery as well. Dignity and honesty come first.
Use real photos of children found online, credited
No consent, and it may endanger or misrepresent the children.

plaibox.win: Do no harm, applied to data. You protected people while still meeting legitimate needs.
plaibox.lose: Revisit responsible-data principles and the green/amber/red rule. Beneficiary data is as precious as the people themselves.

modules.d: A practical, board-ready playbook for responsible AI use across your NGO.
modules.body:
Why a playbook, not just a policy

Many organisations write an AI policy listing prohibitions and stop there. Staff then either ignore AI or use it secretly. A playbook does more: it states what is encouraged, provides approved tools and templates, sets clear data rules, defines review responsibilities, and builds capability. It makes the right way the easy way.

The structure of your playbook

  1. Purpose and principles — why your organisation uses AI and the values that guide it (mission first, do no harm, honesty with donors and communities, human accountability).
  2. Approved use cases — the five to ten priority uses identified in Module 1, with examples.
  3. Approved tools — from your Module 3 evaluation, with the plans and settings to use.
  4. Data rules — the green/amber/red classification with examples, and anonymisation steps.
  5. Quality and verification rules — every figure traced to a source; AI never produces statistics or quotes; human review before any external document is sent.
  6. Disclosure — when and how to disclose AI use to donors, partners and communities.
  7. Roles and responsibilities — an AI focal point, data owners, reviewers, and leadership oversight.
  8. Templates and prompt library — the proposal engine, M&E prompts, reporting templates, communications prompts.
  9. Training plan — onboarding for new staff and refresher sessions.
  10. Monitoring and review — indicators and a review date.
Keep it short enough to be used. A four-to-six-page core playbook with annexes for templates is far more effective than a forty-page document nobody reads. Test it by asking a new staff member to use it for one task.

Getting leadership and board buy-in

Present the playbook as a governance and capacity decision. Show the problem (staff time lost to low-value tasks; risks from unmanaged AI use already happening), the proposal (approved tools, rules, training), the costs, the expected benefits with indicators, and the risks with mitigations. Boards respond to clarity about risk management as much as to promised efficiency.

Implementation in 90 days

Days 1–30: approve the playbook, appoint the focal point, set up approved tools, train all staff on data rules. Days 31–60: roll out two or three priority workflows, such as the proposal engine and qualitative analysis, with coaching. Days 61–90: measure time saved and quality, collect staff feedback, refine templates and report to leadership. Then review the playbook every six to twelve months as tools and laws change.

Measuring success

Use a balanced set of indicators: efficiency (hours per proposal, report turnaround), effectiveness (proposal win rate, report quality ratings from donors), compliance (data incidents, adherence audits), capability (staff confidence and skills), and mission impact (time redirected to field and beneficiaries). Report honestly, including what did not work.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit your organisation's AI playbook (core document of four to six pages), one completed workflow template with a worked example, a 90-day implementation plan, and a one-page board briefing. Your mentor reviews it for practicality, ethics and fit with your context.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my NGO AI playbook editor. Using what I tell you about my organisation, its priority use cases, approved tools and data classification, draft a concise playbook with the ten sections from this module. Keep the core under six pages. Then draft a one-page board briefing with problem, proposal, costs, benefits, risks and indicators, and a 90-day implementation plan with owners.

📚 Glossary

  • Playbook: practical guide enabling responsible use, not just prohibitions
  • AI focal point: person coordinating AI use, training and support
  • Disclosure: informing stakeholders about AI use where relevant or required
  • Balanced indicators: efficiency, effectiveness, compliance, capability and mission impact

📖 References

  • NTEN — AI governance resources for nonprofits.
  • UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
  • NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework.

quiz.q: A Nigerian NGO's AI policy is a two-page list of prohibitions. Six months later, staff either avoid AI or use personal accounts secretly. What does the module recommend?
opts: Add more prohibitions and a disciplinary procedure so that staff follow the existing policy
Build a playbook with approved uses, tools, templates, data rules and training
Remove the policy and let each team decide how to use AI based on its own needs
Ban personal accounts and run a staff survey on AI use every quarter going forward
quiz.x: A playbook goes beyond prohibitions: approved uses, tools, templates, data rules, review roles and training make the right way the easy way. More prohibitions deepen the secret-use problem.

quiz.q: An NGO's AI working group produced a 40-page guide. A recent hire could not find how to use AI for a donor report. Which change does the module advise?
opts: Create a four-to-six-page core playbook with annexes, and test it with a new staff member
Add an index and a glossary so that staff can navigate the full document more easily later
Replace the document with a short video that summarises the main points for staff
Hold a two-day training on the full document so that all staff learn its content well
quiz.x: A four-to-six-page core with annexes for templates is far more effective; test it by asking a new staff member to use it for one task. An index does not fix length.

quiz.q: Presenting an AI playbook to a board in Freetown, the director focuses on efficiency gains. A board member is unconvinced. What else does the module say boards respond to?
opts: A live demonstration of AI drafting a proposal during the board meeting itself
Clear risk management: current unmanaged use, risks with mitigations and governance
A larger budget request showing commitment to digital transformation over five years
A comparison of the AI tools used by other NGOs in the country and their reported results
quiz.x: Boards respond to clarity about risk management as much as to promised efficiency, including the risks of unmanaged AI use already happening. A live demo shows capability but not governance.

quiz.q: In a 90-day rollout, an NGO plans to launch five workflows in month one before naming a focal point or training staff on data rules. How should it be resequenced?
opts: Keep it, since early wins in month one build momentum for the governance work later later
Roll out the workflows in month one but limit them to staff who already use AI
Spend all 90 days on training, then roll out workflows in the following quarter
Days 1-30 approve, appoint and train on data rules; 31-60 roll out two or three workflows
quiz.x: The module's plan: days 1-30 approve the playbook, appoint a focal point, set up tools and train on data rules; days 31-60 roll out two or three priority workflows; days 61-90 measure and refine.

quiz.q: An NGO measures AI success with one number: hours saved. A donor asks whether quality and compliance are also tracked. Which indicator set is closest to the module's balanced approach?
opts: Hours per proposal, win rate, data incidents, staff confidence and time redirected to the field
Hours saved, prompts per staff member and licence costs, reported monthly to the board in full
Number of tools adopted, training sessions held and staff attendance at each session
Report turnaround, donor satisfaction and social media engagement on AI-assisted posts
quiz.x: The balanced set covers efficiency, effectiveness, compliance, capability and mission impact. Turnaround and donor satisfaction cover two dimensions but miss compliance and capability.

quiz.q: A playbook rule says: 'AI may help draft reports.' A reviewer flags a gap in the quality rules. Which addition best reflects the module?
opts: Reports drafted with AI must use the organisation's official template and approved font
AI drafts must be shorter than human drafts to reduce the risk of errors appearing
Figures traced to a source, no AI-made statistics or quotes, human review before sending
Staff must state which AI model they used in the file name of every external document
quiz.x: The quality and verification rules: every figure traced to a source, AI does not produce statistics or quotes, and human review before any external document is sent.

quiz.q: An NGO uses AI heavily in proposals but has no stated position on whether to tell funders or the people it serves. Which playbook section is missing?
opts: Disclosure: when and how to tell donors, partners and communities about AI use
Roles and responsibilities, naming a focal point to oversee proposal quality
Approved tools, listing which AI plans and settings staff may use for proposal drafting
Training plan, covering onboarding for new staff and refresher sessions each year
quiz.x: Disclosure states when and how to disclose AI use to donors, partners and communities. Roles matter but do not answer the honesty question.

quiz.q: After a year, an NGO's AI playbook still names a tool the provider has discontinued and predates a new national data law. What practice was missing?
opts: A rule that staff check the provider's website each month
A larger initial budget so the original tools could be kept
A review every six to twelve months as tools and laws change
A longer playbook covering many more tools in its first edition
quiz.x: The module advises reviewing the playbook every six to twelve months as tools and laws change. Monthly individual checks are not an organisational review with a set date.

quiz.q: Which role does the module recommend appointing so that one person coordinates AI adoption, tools and support across a 30-person NGO?
opts: A board committee that approves each staff request to use an AI tool for a specific task
An AI focal point, alongside named data owners, reviewers and leadership oversight
A full-time AI developer who builds custom tools for each programme team on request
A data protection officer recruited from outside who audits all staff AI use every month
quiz.x: The playbook names an AI focal point plus data owners, reviewers and leadership oversight. Per-task board approval is unworkable and drives secret use.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian NGO submits its capstone: a 5-page playbook and a 90-day plan. The mentor returns it as incomplete. What is most likely missing from the deliverable?
opts: A signed data processing agreement with each AI provider that staff currently use
A full literature review on AI in the nonprofit sector with at least twenty references
A list of every AI tool on the market with a price comparison and a vendor contact list
A completed workflow template with a worked example and a one-page board briefing
quiz.x: The capstone requires the playbook, one completed workflow template with a worked example, a 90-day plan and a one-page board briefing. Signed DPAs may follow but are not the specified deliverable.

facts.t: Sections in the NGO AI playbook.
facts.more: Purpose and principles, use cases, tools, data rules, verification, disclosure, roles, templates and prompt library, training, monitoring and review.

facts.t: Core playbook length, with templates in annexes.
facts.more: A short playbook gets used. Test it by asking a new staff member to complete one task with it.

facts.t: Implementation in three 30-day phases.
facts.more: Approve and train, then roll out 2–3 priority workflows, then measure, refine and report to leadership. Review every 6–12 months.

facts.t: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (2023) organises AI governance into four functions.
facts.more: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. It is a voluntary reference that boards and donors increasingly recognise.

labs.title: The 90-day rollout
steps: Set up approved tools and train all staff on data rules
Roll out the proposal engine and qualitative analysis with coaching
Measure time saved and quality and collect staff feedback
Refine templates and report to leadership
labs.tip: Rules and training come before workflows. Measurement comes before expansion.

labs.title: Indicator and balanced-scorecard dimension
labs.intro: Match each indicator to the dimension it measures.
pairs: Number of data incidents involving AI tools
Share of staff confident using the prompt library
Staff days redirected to field visits
labs.tip: Boards trust a balanced set more than a single efficiency number.

plaibox.title: Board briefing builder
plaibox.intro: Assemble a one-page board briefing for your playbook. Copy it into your AI tool, then make sure every figure comes from your own records.
